title: Depth-first search on a binary search tree

screens.title: Welcome
screens.subtitle: Learn binary search trees and explore how DFS visits nodes, uses a stack and backtracks. Designed for complete beginners.

preview.label: BST + DFS visualisation preview
preview.caption: **Lost in a maze?** Take the left-most passage you have not tried. At a dead end, go back to the last fork and try the next one. That is depth-first search, and here it is on a tree.

outcomes.title: Trace DFS on a tree
outcomes.text: Follow the visit order: go deep on the left, backtrack, then go right.

outcomes.title: Use a stack to track the path
outcomes.text: Push right, then left, and always take the top.

outcomes.title: Tell DFS apart from BST search
outcomes.text: See why DFS ignores the values, and what that costs.

screens.title: What is a Binary Search Tree?
screens.subtitle: Before learning depth-first search, let's understand the structure we will explore.

figure.title: A tree is made of connected nodes
figure.text: The **root** is the starting node. Each node can have **children**. A **leaf** has no children.

side.title: The BST ordering rule
side.note: This rule applies at every node.

quickCheck.prompt: Quick check: where would the number 25 go?

options.feedback: 25 < 50, so go left. 25 < 30, so go left to 20. 25 > 20, so go right. That spot is empty, so 25 goes there.
Close, but 30 already has a left child: 20. Keep comparing: 25 > 20, so 25 becomes the right child of 20.
25 is smaller than 50, so it belongs in the left half of the tree, not under 70.

screens.title: Depth-First Search: go deep, then backtrack
screens.subtitle: Remember the maze on the home page? DFS does the same thing in a tree. Learn the idea before the step-by-step explorer.

side.title: How DFS works
items: Explore one branch as deeply as possible.
Backtrack when you reach a dead end.
Continue until the search is complete.
side.note: Our DFS explores left before right. Going back up is called **backtracking**.

quickCheck.prompt: Quick check: DFS has just visited 20, a leaf. Which node does it visit next?

options.feedback: 20 is a dead end, so DFS backtracks to 30 and goes down its unexplored right side: 40.
70 is still waiting. DFS first finishes everything under 30, so 40 comes before 70.
DFS does not restart at the root. It goes back to the most recent node with an unexplored child (30) and visits 40.

screens.title: How DFS remembers: the stack
screens.subtitle: To backtrack, DFS has to remember which nodes it still needs to explore. It keeps them on a stack. First, a quick check on stacks.

quickCheck.prompt: Warm-up: you push 1, then 2, then 3 onto a stack. Which number comes off first?

options.feedback: 1 went on first, so it is at the bottom. A stack gives back the *last* item you put on.
2 is in the middle. A stack only lets you take the top item.
The last one in is the first one out. DFS relies on exactly this.

quickCheck.refresher: **Refresher:** a **stack** is like a pile of plates. You can only put a plate on top (**push**) or take the top plate off (**pop**). The last plate you put on is the first one you take off.

figure.title: Watch the stack
figure.text: Step through a search for 60. Watch what goes on the stack, and what comes off.

side.title: Push right, then left

items.heading: DFS keeps a stack.
items.text: It holds the nodes DFS still has to explore.

items.heading: Leaving a node: push its children.
The left child is on top.
items.text: It went on last, so it comes off first.

side.note: That is why DFS always explores the left side first.

screens.title: The four steps
screens.subtitle: The whole search fits in four steps. Here they are in plain English and in Java, the way you will see them in COS212.

figure.title: DFS search in Java
figure.text: The numbers in the comments match the four steps on the right.
lines: if (root != null) stack.push(root);           // 1. push the root
TreeNode current = stack.pop();           // 2. pop and visit
return false;                                 // 4. stack empty: not there

side.title: In plain English
items: Push the root onto the stack.
Pop the top node and **visit** it.
If it is the target, stop. Otherwise push its right child, then its left child, skipping empty ones.
If the stack is empty, stop: the value is not in the tree. Otherwise go back to step 2.

quickCheck.prompt: Quick check: DFS pops 30, which is not the target. Its children are 20 (left) and 40 (right). What does it push, in order?

options.feedback: Right first, then left. 20 ends up on top, so it is explored next.
That would leave 40 on top, and DFS would explore the right side first. Push right first, so left is on top.
When a node is not the target, DFS pushes its children so it can explore them later.

screens.title: Three orders, one walk
screens.subtitle: DFS can also list every value in a tree. The walk is always the same. What changes is *when* you write a node down.

figure.title: Try each order
figure.text: Choose an order, then step through it. Run **in-order** to the end: notice anything?

afterRun.IN_ORDER: **It is sorted!** In a BST everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is larger, so "left, node, right" always lists the values from smallest to largest.

side.title: When to write a node down

items.heading: Pre-order
items.text: When you first arrive, before its children.

items.heading: In-order
items.text: After its left side, before its right side.

items.heading: Post-order
items.text: When you leave it for the last time, after both sides.

side.note: Same walk, same tree: only the moment of writing changes.

quickCheck.prompt: Quick check: which order lists the values of a BST from smallest to largest?

options.feedback: Pre-order writes the root first, and the root is not the smallest value.
Left side (smaller), then the node, then the right side (larger): sorted every time.
Post-order writes the root last, and the root is not the largest value.

screens.title: What DFS does not do
screens.subtitle: DFS does not look at the values to decide where to go. Even when the target is bigger than the root, it explores the whole left side first.

figure.title: Search for 80 with DFS
figure.text: 80 is bigger than 50, but watch where DFS goes first.
figure.caption: DFS needed **{nodesVisited} visits** to find 80. BST search would need only 3.

side.title: DFS is not BST search

items.heading: DFS ignores the values.
items.text: It always explores left first, whatever the target is.

items.heading: BST search uses them.
items.text: Looking for 80: 80 > 50, go right; 80 > 70, go right. Found in 3 visits: 50, 70, 80.

side.note: You will meet BST search in the lecture. Keep this difference in mind.

quickCheck.prompt: Quick check: DFS is searching tree A for 80. At the root (50), where does it go first?

options.feedback: DFS always goes left first. It never compares 80 with 50 to choose a direction.
That is the BST search rule. DFS ignores the values and explores the left side first.

screens.title: Explore DFS, step by step
screens.subtitle: Watch the visited nodes, the stack and the visit order change as you explore.

example.intro: **Worked example.** DFS searches this tree for 60. Press **Search**, then **Next step** to move one step at a time. Watch the stack on the right: the node on top is always the next one visited.

own.intro: **Your own tree.** Insert values, search for any number, or run a traversal. Before each run, predict the visit order, then check it.

screens.doneMessage: **You followed the whole search.** Now try it on a tree you build yourself.
screens.lockedNote: Try your own tree unlocks after you finish the worked example.

screens.title: Your turn: predict the next node
screens.subtitle: Try a search on your own. The tutor gives hints whenever you need them.
screens.questionHint: Think about the stack before choosing your answer. You can also click the node on the tree.
screens.finishText: Next: list the whole tree in in-order, below.
screens.worked: A few steps needed the full answer. Replaying the worked example may help.

orderTask.title: Practice 2: put the nodes in in-order
orderTask.text: Click the nodes in in-order (left side, node, right side), or type them. Hint: for a BST the answer is sorted.
orderTask.correct: **Correct.** In-order of a BST always comes out sorted. You are ready for the quiz.
orderTask.wrong: Remember: everything left of a node comes before it, and everything right of it comes after.

lecture.title: Prepare for lecture
lecture.text: Questions to think about before the lecture.

lectureQuestions: DFS needed 6 visits to find 60 in tree A. Using the BST rule (smaller left, larger right) you would need only 3. How would that search work, and what is its worst case?
When might you want to explore a tree level by level (breadth-first) instead of depth-first?
Our DFS uses an explicit stack. How would you write the same search with recursion, and where does the stack go?
